newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China dissidents in HK cancel hunger strike plan.
newsitem.headline: China dissidents in HK cancel hunger strike plan.

text.p: A group of Chinese dissidents stranded in Hong Kong have cancelled a planned hunger strike over demands to leave before China takes over, activists said on Tuesday.
The group of about eight, among 40 or so dissidents who have fled from the mainland, accuse the Hong Kong government of refusing to aid them escape Beijing's rule from July 1.
One threatened suicide by setting himself on fire unless the government replied to demands to help them leave for sanctuary abroad by a May 27 deadline.
Western countries are reported set to grant asylum to Chinese dissidents living in exile here and fearing communist persecution after China takes Hong Kong back from Britain.
But officials here and diplomats have covered any rescue plans with a cloak of secrecy.
The eight, demanding faster action to clear their uncertain status, announced a protest-fast against local bureaucracy.
A human rights group said they called it off after a Hong Kong government offer on Monday to discuss their immigration status.
The Information Centre of Human Rights and the Democratic Movement in China, an umbrella group, has taken up the plight of all the dissidents.
Reports say two have been offered asylum by European countries but want to go to North America, five have yet to prove their dissident status and one has arranged to leave shortly.
About 40 dissidents are stranded in Hong Kong, their future uncertain. Most fled China illegally and arrived in Hong Kong without a right of automatic residency.
Fifteen are said to be discussing offers of asylum from Finland, Denmark, Canada and the United States.
Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten chided the small group upon his return from London on Monday, saying threats and ultimatums were inappropriate.

"I hope the ... people who sent the ultimatum will recognise that the way to deal with these sensitive and complicated issues isn't by making threats or by delivering so-called ultimatums," Patten told reporters.

The fears of remaining exiles intensified in recent months as China unveiled plans to roll back democracy and human rights legislation in Hong Kong under British rule and vowed to check "anti-constitutional" activities.
Hundreds of Chinese dissidents and pro-democracvy activists fled after army tanks thundered into Beijing's Tiananmen Square in June, 1989, crushing a student-led democracy movement.
Many of the fugitives found sanctuary in Hong Kong and then were discreetly resettled in the West.

The remaining handful got an assurance on Tuesday from a pro-China politician and member of the Provisional Legislature which will take power upon the handover of the British colony of Hong Kong at midnight on June 30.
Maria Tam, co-founder of the New Hong Kong Progressive Alliance, said the dissidents should not face prosecution for activities that were not illegal in Hong Kong at the time.
Chinese law did not apply in Hong Kong before the handover and dissidents would be safe if they refrained from breaking the law after July 1.
But prominent dissident Han Dongfang early this month warned fellow political exiles here they risked arrest by China on criminal charges linked to border offences.
